rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from urging self-sacrifice in jihad to urging financial sacrifice and warning those who withhold wealth in God's cause.
rows.anchor: لما بالغ في التحريض على بذل النفس في الجهاد في الآيات المتقدمة شرع ههنا في التحريض على بذل المال

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: For Hamza's second-person reading, the construction means do not consider the stinginess of the stingy good for them; a noun for stinginess is elided because the verb supplies it.
rows.anchor: بالتاء والباقون بالياء ، أما قراءة حمزة بالتاء المنقطة من فوق فقال الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the other readers' third-person form, the subject may be the Prophet or anyone in general, or the stingy themselves with the object their stinginess omitted.
rows.anchor: أن يكون فاعل { يحسبن } ضمير رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ، أو ضمير أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object is licensed by context, as in the saying about lying being bad and the phrase about a fool running toward folly; al-Farra's verse uses به for kingship, inferable from kings.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الفراء هم الملوك وأبناء الملوك هم والآخذون به والسادة الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basrans call هو a separating pronoun and Kufans a support; it marks the added relation in which the subject is predicated of the predicate.
rows.anchor: هو في قوله : { هو خيرا لهم } تسميه البصريون فصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned stinginess can concern any good or benefit, including either wealth or knowledge.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن الآية دالة على ذم البخل بشيء من الخيرات والمنافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view applies the warning to withholding wealth: the withheld money will become punishment, while the money itself will not remain with them because God inherits all.
rows.anchor: القول الأول : ان هذا الوعيد ورد على البخل بالمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view applies it to withholding knowledge: Jews concealed Muhammad's description and the glad tidings of his coming in the Torah and Gospel, although knowledge is God's gift.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أن المراد من هذا البخل : البخل بالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers wealth: the collar threat fits money literally, whereas knowledge requires metaphor; reading wealth also continues the preceding exhortation to spend in jihad, unlike the knowledge reading.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن القول الأول أولى ، ويدل عليه وجهان

rows.speaker: أكثر العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars define stinginess as withholding what is obligatory, not declining voluntary giving: the severe threat and blame fit neglected duties, not optional generosity.
rows.anchor: أكثر العلماء على أن البخل عبارة عن منع الواجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proofs include that God cannot give without limit, so refusing any extra favor cannot make Him stingy; a hadith calls stinginess a dreadful disease, and withholding voluntary gifts would not warrant that label.
rows.anchor: قال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( وأي داء أدوأ من البخل ) ومعلوم أن تارك التطوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If every refusal of a voluntary gift were stinginess, even the owner of all wealth could escape the charge only by giving everything; 2:3 praises spending only part of God's provision and 2:5 calls such people guided and successful.
rows.anchor: { ومما رزقناهم ينفقون } ( البقرة : 3 ) وكلمة ( من ) للتبعيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obligatory spending includes one's own needs and dependents, zakat, defense when Muslims face an attack on lives or property, and enough aid to keep a desperate person alive; withholding these is stinginess.
rows.anchor: إذا صار أحد من المسلمين مضطرا فانه يجب عليه أن يدفع اليه مقدار ما يستبقي به رمقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal interpretation makes the withheld wealth a tormenting collar: it may become snakes around the neck and body, or a collar of fire; the neck image fits unpaid zakat, and the body image fits hoarded property.
rows.anchor: أن يحمل هذا على ظاهره وهو أنه تعالى يطوقهم بطوق يكون سببا لعذابهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says withheld zakat will become a two-spotted serpent collar that bites the miser's cheeks and says it is the zakat he withheld in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : تجعل تلك الزكاة الممنوعة في عنقهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the collar as being required at resurrection to produce what one withheld, when compliance is impossible, as a reproach for not giving it when able.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : سيكلفون أن يأتوا بما بخلوا به يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn Abbas in 2:184 understands the duty as something they are burdened with but cannot bear, supporting Mujahid's interpretation of the impossible demand.
rows.anchor: أنه كان يقرأ { وعلى الذين * يطيقونه فدية } ( البقرة : 184 ) قال المفسرون : يكلفونه ولا يطيقونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A figurative reading says they will carry the sin of stinginess; Arabic represents an emphatically imposed burden as being placed around someone's neck, as in the statement about each person's deeds.
rows.anchor: القول الثالث : أن قوله : { سيطوقون ما بخلوا به } أي سيلزمون إثمه في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If stinginess means concealing knowledge, the collar is a fiery bridle on the mouths and tongues that failed to speak the truth; a prophetic report threatens such a bridle for concealing known knowledge.
rows.anchor: من سئل عن علم يعلمه فكتمه ألجمه الله بلجام من النار يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The knowledge interpretation is plausible because the Quran also condemns Jewish stinginess, and the next verse cites a Jewish statement; the warning may cover withholding both knowledge and wealth.
rows.anchor: ولا يبعد أيضا أن تكون الآية عامة في البخل بالعلم ، وفي البخل بالمال

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Mu'tazilites cite the verse as a decisive threat against grave sinners: it promises loss of reward and fire and explicitly says the withheld thing will be collared at resurrection.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : هذه الآية دالة على القطع بوعيد الفساق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's inheritance means either all that the inhabitants of heaven and earth own, making their withholding from Him pointless, or, according to most, God's sole ownership after all creatures die; Razi reports Ibn al-Anbari's linguistic point that inheritance can mean exclusive possession after sharing, as in Solomon's inheritance of David.
rows.anchor: والثاني : وهو قول الأكثرين : المراد أنه يفنى أهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read the final verb in the third person, referring to the misers whose denial of rights God knows and will punish; the other readers address the audience directly, continuing the preceding second-person address.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو { بما يعملون } بالياء على المغايبة كناية عن الذين يبخلون

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf calls the third-person reading a rhetorical shift of address and says it intensifies the threat.
rows.anchor: الياء على طريقة الالتفات وهي أبلغ في الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After extended legal discussion and answers to opponents, the passage redirects hearts from created things toward knowing God, using the signs of divine unity, divinity, majesty, and greatness.
rows.anchor: جذب القلوب والأرواح عن الاشتغال بالخلق إلى الاستغراق في معرفة الحق

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports Aisha's account that the Prophet asked permission for night worship, prayed and wept, then said this verse had been revealed that night and asked whether he should not be a grateful servant.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عمر : قلت لعائشة : أخبريني بأعجب ما رأيت من رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic warning says woe to anyone who recites the verse without reflecting on it; another wording warns against merely chewing it between the jaws without contemplation.
rows.anchor: ويل لمن قرأها ولم يتفكر فيها . وروي : ويل لمن لاكها بين فكيه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali reports that when the Prophet rose at night, he used a toothstick, looked toward the sky, and recited the verse.
rows.anchor: وعن علي رضي الله عنه : أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان اذا قام من الليل يتسوك ثم ينظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Israelite youth's cloud of shade failed to appear during worship; his mother suggested he had once looked at the sky without reflecting, and he recalled doing so.
rows.anchor: قالت : لعلك نظرة مرة إلى السماء ولم تعتبر قال نعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse repeats three signs from 2:164, whereas that passage lists eight and ends with people who reason; this difference raises questions about repetition, omitted signs, and the phrase possessors of intellect.
rows.anchor: وختم هذه الآية في سورة البقرة بقوله : { لآيات لقوم يعقلون } ( البقرة : 164 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart's inner eye cannot focus fully on two objects at once: beginners need many proofs, but once divine knowledge illuminates the heart, fewer proofs allow fuller absorption in God.
rows.anchor: السالك إلى الله لا بد له في أول الأمر من تكثير الدلائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' command to remove his sandals in 20:12 alludes to leaving behind the premises that lead reason to knowledge when entering the sacred valley of divine oneness.
rows.anchor: والنعلان هما المقدمتان اللتان بهما يتوصل العقل إلى المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eight signs in 2:164 suit an initial seeker; repeating only three celestial signs here, and omitting five earthly ones, signals that the realized knower should reduce attention to proofs, while heavenly signs are more overwhelming and wondrous.
rows.anchor: فذكر في سورة البقرة ثمانية أنواع من الدلائل ، ثم أعاد في هذه السورة ثلاثة أنواع منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shifts from people who reason to possessors of intellect because reason has an outward and an inner core: the first stage is intellect, and its completed state is the core.
rows.anchor: لأن العقل له ظاهر وله لب ، ففي أول الأمر يكون عقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance is not accepted once death's signs and terrors arrive, as shown also by the rejected belief of Pharaoh at drowning and by the deathbed pleas in other passages.
rows.anchor: الآية دالة على أن من حضره الموت وشاهد أهواله فان توبته غير مقبولة

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب
rows.claim: Abu Ayyub transmits from the Prophet that God accepts a servant's repentance until the soul reaches the throat and rattles there.
rows.anchor: روى أبو أيوب عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن الله تعالى يقبل توبة العبد ما لم يغرغر

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says repentance is accepted even until a moment before death, as short as the time it takes a camel to be milked.
rows.anchor: وعن عطاء : ولو قبل موته بفواق الناقة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan relates that Satan vowed to mislead Adam's children while their souls remained in their bodies, and God vowed to keep repentance open until the soul rattles in the throat.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن : أن ابليس قال حين أهبط إلى الأرض : وعزتك لا أفارق ابن آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When death comes means when its signs and approach are present, as in the command about an inheritance when death comes in 2:180.
rows.anchor: { حتى إذا حضر أحدهم الموت } ( النساء : 18 ) أي علامات نزول الموت وقربه

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The investigators say nearness to death and its pain do not itself bar repentance; the true barrier is witnessing events that make knowledge of God unavoidable and remove moral responsibility.
rows.anchor: قال المحققون : قرب الموت لا يمنع من قبول التوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People revived after death, including Israelites and Job's children, were again charged with duties, so experiencing death does not itself end accountability.
rows.anchor: أن جماعة أماتهم الله تعالى ثم أحياهم مثل قوم من بنى إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death's pains resemble colic or labor, which do not end responsibility; rising distress should make repentance more likely to be accepted, since God responds to the distressed in 27:62.
rows.anchor: وهو تعالى يقول : { أمن يجيب المضطر إذا دعاه } ( النمل : 62 ) فتزايد الآلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At death, witnessed terrors make knowledge of God necessary and end obligation; people of the afterlife likewise cannot repent even before entering Hell because their knowledge is necessary.
rows.anchor: ومتى صارت معرفته بالله ضرورية سقط التكليف عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi challenges the Mu'tazilite claim that resurrection makes knowledge of God necessary: observing revival and fire does not prove God caused them, since those conclusions remain inferential.
rows.anchor: فكيف يمكن ادعاء أن أهل الآخرة لأجل مشاهدة أهوالها يعرفون الله بالضرورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if resurrection knowledge were necessary, the Mu'tazilites have not shown why that ends duty: a servant might still sin while believing God is merciful and unaffected by human obedience.
rows.anchor: فلم قلتم بأن العلم بالله إذا كان ضروريا منع من صحة التكليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their distinction between theoretical and necessary knowledge is weak: if the possibility of the opposite remains, there is only opinion; if it does not, theoretical knowledge cannot be weaker than necessary knowledge.
rows.anchor: امتنع أن يكون علم آخر أقوى منه وآكد منه ، وعلى هذا التقدير لا يبقى ألبتة فرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God acts as He wills: by grace He promised acceptance at some times and by justice announced rejection at another, and He can reverse either judgment, as 21:23 says.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن هذه الأشياء التي تذكرها المعتزلة كلمات ضعيفة واهية ، وأنه تعالى يفعل ما يشاء ويحكم ما يريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A three-part division follows: repentance from ignorant sin is promised acceptance in 4:17; repentance only at death is rejected; deliberate sinners who repent earlier are left to God's will, as in 4:48.
rows.anchor: فلما كان القسم الأول : هم الذين يعملون السوء بجهالة ، والقسم الثاني : هم الذين لا يتوبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about those who die as disbelievers can mean people near death, whose faith too is rejected, or unbelievers who die in disbelief and cannot repent in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: المراد أن الكفار إذا ماتوا على الكفر فلو تابوا في الآخرة لا تقبل توبتهم

rows.speaker: الوعيدية
rows.claim: Threat proponents argue that the conjunction separates sinners who repent at death from disbelievers, yet the same painful threat covers both; they also say forgiveness without repentance would make the warning pointless.
rows.anchor: تعلقت الوعيدية بهذه الآية على صحة مذهبهم من وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that the nearest referent of the prepared painful punishment can be disbelievers alone; because their unbelief is worse, they may receive added humiliation beyond sinful believers.
rows.anchor: فلم لا يجوز أن يكون قوله : { أعتدنا لهم عذابا أليما } عائدا إلى الكفار فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The absence of repentance at death still leaves punishment or forgiveness possible and thus warns the sinner, like 4:48; moreover, the Mu'tazilites themselves reject arguments from what a text merely implies.
rows.anchor: أما الوجه الثاني : مما عولوا عليه : فهو أنه أخبر أنه لا توبة عند المعاينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because disbelievers are conjoined separately from those who sin, the verse refutes the Kharijite claim that a Muslim sinner is an unbeliever; the hypocrite reading also fails because hypocrites are unbelievers, as 63:1 says.
rows.anchor: المسألة الخامسة : أنه تعالى عطف على الذين يتوبون عند مشاهدة الموت ، الكفار

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Aʿtadna means prepared or made ready; the past tense in 4:18 and the parallel descriptions of Hell in 2:24 and 3:131 are used to argue that Hell is already created.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا بهذه الآية على أن النار مخلوقة

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Quraysh leaders asked Muhammad to dismiss poor believers such as Suhayb, Khabbab, Bilal, and Ammar so they might follow him; he refused, then agreed to separate meeting times in hope they would convert.
rows.anchor: روي عن عبدالله بن مسعود أنه قال : مر الملأ من قريش على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the leaders demanded a written agreement and Umar suggested trying their request, this verse descended; the Prophet threw away the page, Umar apologized, and Salman and Khabbab said it concerned them.
rows.anchor: فنزلت هذه الآية ، فرمى الصحيفة ، واعتذر عمر عن مقالته

rows.speaker: سلمان وخباب
rows.claim: Salman and Khabbab say the Prophet then sat with them until his knees touched theirs; after 18:28 he stopped rising before them and praised God for being commanded to stay with them in life and death.
rows.anchor: فنزل قوله { واصبر نفسك مع الذين يدعون ربهم } ( الكهف : 28 ) فترك القيام عنا إلى أن نقوم عنه

rows.speaker: الطاعنون في عصمة الأنبياء
rows.claim: Critics cite the incident as sin: the Prophet expelled poor believers despite the prohibition, became one of the wrongdoers, contradicted Noah's refusal to expel believers and the command to follow prophets, sought worldly adornment, and later said God rebuked him.
rows.anchor: احتج الطاعنون في عصمة الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says Muhammad did not dismiss them from contempt for poverty; he set separate meeting times to win Quraysh, whose conversion mattered greatly, and any mistaken judgment in this effort is forgiven.
rows.anchor: ما طردهم لأجل الاستخفاف بهم والاستنكاف من فقرهم وإنما عين لجلوسهم وقتا معينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling their dismissal wrongful means the poor deserved honor; expelling them from that gathering wronged them by leaving the more fitting and excellent course, not by violating a duty. The other criticisms likewise concern what was preferable.
rows.anchor: كان ذلك ظلما ، إلا أنه من باب ترك الأولى والأفضل لا من باب ترك الواجبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Amir reads بالغدوة with waw and a damma on ghayn, also in 18:28; the other readers have the common form بالغداة with alif and a fatha.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر { بالغداة والعشى } بالواو وضم الغين وفي سورة الكهف مثله

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Farisi favors the common reading because ghadāh is an indefinite noun that can take the definite article, while ghudwah is a proper name; spelling ṣalāh with waw despite its alif sound shows orthography proves nothing.
rows.anchor: الوجه قراءة العامة بالغدة لأنها تستعمل نكرة فأمكن تعريفها بإدخال لام التعريف عليها

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says ghudwah and bukrah can function as generic names like Umm Hubayn; Yunus reports Abu Amr leaves them uninflected when used definitely, supporting the common reading, while al-Khalil permits them like ḍuḥwah, supporting Ibn Amir.
rows.anchor: زعم الخليل أنه يجوز أن يقال أتيتك اليوم غدوة وبكرة فجعلهما بمنزلة ضحوة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Hasan, and Mujahid take calling upon God at dawn and evening to mean the prescribed dawn and afternoon prayers; another explanation treats the two ends of the day as shorthand for keeping all five prayers.
rows.anchor: أن المراد من الدعاء الصلاة ، يعني يعبدون ربهم بالصلاة المكتوبة

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim takes الدعاء to mean remembrance: the poor believers remember God at the two ends of the day.
rows.anchor: قال إبراهيم : الدعاء ههنا هو الذكر والمعنى يذكرون ربهم طرفي النهار

rows.speaker: المجسمة
rows.claim: The anthropomorphists cite wanting God's face and related verses such as 55:27 as evidence that God has bodily parts; Razi answers that God's complete oneness in 112:1 rules out composition.
rows.anchor: المجسمة تمسكوا في إثبات الأعضاء لله تعالى بقوله { يريدون وجهه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Face is either an honorific way to refer to God Himself, like face of an argument, or a metonym for love and seeking approval because a lover wants to see the beloved's face; compare 2:115.
rows.anchor: جعل الوجه كناية عن المحبة وطلب الرضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes the pronouns in the account clause refer to the disbelievers: the Prophet need not bear their account or worry whether the proposed meeting leads them to Islam, since God guides and governs them.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول : أنه عائد إلى المشركين ، والمعنى ما عليك من حساب المشركين من شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more apparent reading refers the account pronouns to the poor worshippers, since the pronoun in the warning about expelling them certainly refers to those believers and the nearby pronouns should match.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أن الضمير عائد إلى الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي ، وهم الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers accused the poor of joining for food and clothes rather than faith; if so, Muhammad need only judge appearances, while their hidden account belongs to them, as no bearer carries another's burden.
rows.anchor: إن الكفار طعنوا في إيمان أولئك الفقراء وقالوا يا محمد إنهم إنما اجتمعوا عندك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both clauses are needed to express one reciprocal point: neither Muhammad nor the poor will be held responsible for the other's account.
rows.anchor: جعلت الجملتان بمنزلة جملة واحدة قصد بهما معنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is that Muhammad bears no responsibility for their livelihood and they bear none for his; God provides for both, so he should let them remain rather than expel them.
rows.anchor: ما عليك من حساب رزقهم من شيء فتملهم وتطردهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode resembles Noah's exchange with his people over his low-status followers: 26:111-113 describes laborers and craftsmen, and their account belongs to God. The expulsion clause answers the denial; being unjust may mean wronging himself or the poor who deserved welcome.
rows.anchor: وقوله { فتطردهم } جواب النفي ومعناه ، ما عليك من حسابهم من شيء فتطردهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues from the statement that God was never absent that He is exalted above place and direction; if God were on the Throne, He would be absent from elsewhere.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على كونه تعالى متعاليا عن المكان والجهة ، لأنه تعالى قال : { وما كنا غائبين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative that God was present only through knowledge and encompassing awareness is figurative, Razi says, since the wording should first be taken literally; absence and presence also presuppose a place, so neither term applies to what cannot occupy a place.
rows.anchor: الغائب هو الذي يعقل أن يحضر بعد غيبة ، وذلك مشروط بكونه مختصا بمكان وجهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weighing follows the questioning and accounting described earlier; the phrase can be parsed with يومئذ as an adverb and الحق as predicate, or as predicate with الحق describing a just weighing.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنه تعالى لما بين في الآية الأولى أن من جملة أحوال القيامة السؤال والحساب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One literal view says God sets up a balance with a pointer and two pans; Ibn Abbas says the believer's deeds appear in their best form and good deeds outweigh evil, as in 21:47.
rows.anchor: في الخبر أنه تعالى ينصب ميزانا له لسان وكفتان يوم القيامة يوزن به أعمال العباد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a believer's deeds are transformed into a beautiful image for weighing, while most exegetes instead say the weighed items are the written records; a prophetic answer to what is weighed is reported as the records.
rows.anchor: وأما كيفية وزن الأعمال على هذا القول ففيه وجوه : أحدهما : أن أعمال المؤمن تتصور بصورة حسنة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
rows.claim: Ibn Salam describes a balance between jinn and humans facing the Throne, with one pan toward Paradise and one toward Hell, large enough to hold the heavens and earth, watched by Gabriel.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد لله بن سلام ، أن ميزان رب العالمين ينصب بين الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports a man whose 99 scrolls of sins, each as long as sight, are outweighed by a tiny card bearing the testimony that none is god but God and Muhammad is His messenger.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنه ، قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( يأتى برجل يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan reports that when Aisha asked about people remembering one another at resurrection, the Prophet said they would be barefoot and unclothed and too occupied with records and weighing to remember anyone, citing 80:37.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن : بينما الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم ذات يوم واضع رأسه في حجر عائشة

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a huge, voracious drinker may have no weight even equal to a gnat.
rows.anchor: وعن عبيد بن عمير يأتى بالرجل العظيم الأكول الشروب فلا يكون له وزن بعوضة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك والأعمش
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A'mash, followed by many later scholars, take the balance as justice and judgment rather than a literal scale.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : وهو قول مجاهد والضحاك والأعمش ، أن المراد من الميزان العدل والقضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of the figurative reading say weight can mean justice because worldly fairness in taking and giving is shown by weights; Arabic also uses weight figuratively for worth and equality, as in 18:105.
rows.anchor: فلأن العدل في الأخذ والإعطاء ، لا يظهر إلا بالكيل والوزن في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem cited by the author uses ميزانه for the balance of an opponent's argument: the speaker had a measure for every disputant, meaning a reply of equal force, not a physical scale.
rows.anchor: قد كنت قبل لقائكم ذا قوة … عندي لكل مخاصم ميزانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi insists the verse must mean only justice: deeds are transient accidents, so cannot be weighed; even if they persisted, weighing is useless because believers already know God's justice and others could suspect a staged result.
rows.anchor: لأن أعمال العباد أعراض وهي قد فنيت وعدمت ، ووزن المعدوم محال

rows.speaker: أصحاب القول الأول
rows.claim: Literal-scale proponents answer that everyone knows God is just and the scale publicly displays the result: a favorable balance increases joy, an unfavorable one increases grief and shame; some describe light or darkness, others a tilted pan.
rows.anchor: والفائدة في وضع ذلك الميزان أن يظهر ذلك الرجحان لأهل القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi finds several actual balances more apparent than one, citing 21:47 and the verse's plural; separate balances may measure heart, bodily, and spoken acts.
rows.anchor: الأظهر إثبات موازين في يوم القيامة لا ميزان واحد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the plural either as Arabic using a plural for one object or as referring to the things weighed, meaning deeds rather than balances; Razi says both abandon the plain plural despite no obstacle to multiple scales.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : إنما جمع الله الموازين ههنا ، فقال : { فمن ثقلت موازينه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavy and light balances divide humanity into two groups: those whose good deeds exceed their bad and those whose bad exceed their good; no group has equal totals.
rows.anchor: أنها تدل على أن أهل القيامة فريقان منهم من يزيد حسناته

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify those whose balances are light as unbelievers, because being described as wronging God's signs means denying them.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين المراد من قوله : { ومن خفت موازينه } الكافر

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi's al-Basit reports that the Prophet's prayer-card can outweigh a believer's weak good deeds; the wider scholarly report instead gives the card bearing the testimony of faith, which al-Qadi says must be paired with its obligations to avoid encouraging sin.
rows.anchor: وهذا الخبر رواه الواحدي في ( البسيط )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every nation or person has a fixed term; when it arrives death is unavoidable, a warning intended to strengthen observance of religious duties.
rows.anchor: بين أن لكل أحد أجلا معينا لا يتقدم ولا يتأخر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Hasan, and Muqatil say each nation that rejected its messenger was given a deadline until it deserved the decisive destruction appointed for it; Razi prefers this reading because the verse says every nation, not every person.
rows.anchor: القول الأول : وهو قول ابن عباس ، والحسن ومقاتل أن المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the nation-wide deadline is stronger than the lifespan reading: it fits the wording and need not imply that every nation, including Muhammad's community, actually receives total extermination.
rows.anchor: لأن الأمة هي الجماعة في كل زمان ، ومعلوم من حالها التقارب في الأجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the term means an individual's lifespan, a person killed dies at the appointed time; this does not make God unable to lengthen or shorten life, but states what He has decreed rather than making Him an involuntary cause.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد منه أنه تعالى لا يقدر على تبقيته أزيد من ذلك ، ولا أنقص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not advancing or delaying even an hour means no delay or precedence by any smaller amount; an hour is named as the smallest named unit of time.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه تعالى ذكر الساعة لأن هذا اللفظ أقل أسماء الأوقات

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Kalbi say the spending passage was revealed about twelve leading Quraysh who financed the army at Badr.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل والكلبي : نزلت في المطعمين يوم بدر

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid say it concerned Abu Sufyan financing war against Muhammad at Uhud; al-Kashshaf reports he hired two thousand Abyssinians and other Arabs and spent forty uqiyyas, each of forty-two mithqals.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد : نزلت في أبي سفيان وإنفاقه المال على حرب محمد يوم أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers spent to block others from following Muhammad, God's path, even if they did not understand their own purpose in those terms; the spending ultimately became regret because it failed and they were defeated, as 58:21 promises.
rows.anchor: كان غرضهم في الإنفاق الصد عن اتباع محمد وهو سبيل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse specifies those who remained disbelievers because some of the original spenders later became Muslims; its wording appears to restrict their gathering to Hell, and Razi says their spending brings only worldly regret and frustration plus severe punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: بل ذكر أن الذين بقوا على الكفر يكونون كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says God separates the evil unbelieving party from the good believers, then piles the evil together like the crowded mass in 72:19; those refers to the evil party.
rows.anchor: القول الأول : ليميز الله الفريق الخبيث من الكفار من الفريق الطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three are conjoined to the Prophet, emigrants, and Helpers whose repentance was accepted; being named alongside the Prophet raises their standing and places their acceptance in the same account.
rows.anchor: والفائدة في هذا العطف أنا بينا أن من ضم ذكر توبته إلى توبة النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three are those deferred in 9:106; خلفوا need not mean their staying was ordered or approved, but can simply state that they remained behind, perhaps despite a prohibition.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد أن هؤلاء أمروا بالتخلف ، أو حصل الرضا من الرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that the three intended to go to battle but received time to gather equipment; when they delayed through laxity, the Prophet left them behind.
rows.anchor: لا يمتنع أن هؤلاء الثلاثة كانوا على عزيمة الذهاب إلى الغزو فأذن لهم الرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام قدر ما يحصل الآلات

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: A third explanation takes خلفوا to mean that their repentance was deferred after the first group; Ka'b ibn Malik says it refers to the Messenger delaying his judgment, as with those deferred to God's command in 9:106.
rows.anchor: قال كعب بن مالك وهو أحد هؤلاء الثلاثة : قول الله تعالى في حقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source notes variants: خلفوا can mean they were left in Medina behind the fighters and derives from successor or stale-mouth terms; Ja'far al-Sadiq reads خالفوا, and al-A'mash reads المخلفين.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر الصادق { * خالفوا } وقرأ الأعمش وعلى الثلاثة المخلفين
